pages.summary: Distances between the rows of matrices.
body: `pdist` gives the distance between each pair of rows of X, as a row in the order (1,2), (1,3), ..., (2,3), ...; `squareform` turns that row into the symmetric matrix and back. `pdist2` gives the distance from each row of X to each row of Y, or only the K smallest (or largest) in each column with the rows they come from. The distance is Euclidean unless named: `'squaredeuclidean'`, `'seuclidean'` (scaled by each column's standard deviation), `'cityblock'`, `'minkowski'`, `'chebychev'`, `'mahalanobis'`, `'cosine'`, `'correlation'`, `'spearman'`, `'hamming'`, `'jaccard'`, or a function of one's own.

examples.title: Four points, three distances
examples.code:
X = [0 0; 3 4; 6 0; 3 0];
d = pdist(X)
squareform(d)
pdist(X, 'cityblock')
[D, I] = pdist2(X, [3 1; 0 5], 'euclidean', 'Smallest', 2)

pages.summary: Nearest neighbours: the k nearest points, and all points within a distance.
body: `knnsearch` gives, for each row of Y, the k rows of X nearest it (nearest first) and their distances; `rangesearch` gives, as cells, the rows within r. Distances are Euclidean unless named. A searcher made once (`createns`, or `KDTreeSearcher` and `ExhaustiveSearcher` directly) holds X and its distance for many searches; the answers are the same either way.

examples.title: Shops near two homes

pages.summary: The squared Mahalanobis distance of points from a sample.
body: (y - mu) inv(C) (y - mu)', mu and C the mean and covariance of the sample's rows: distance measured in standard deviations along the sample's own directions, so that a point off a correlated cloud's axis is far even when it is near in plain distance. For a Gaussian mixture, a column for each component.
syntax: From each component of a mixture.

examples.title: Two points at the same plain distance

pages.summary: k clusters, each about its centroid, or about one of its own points.
body: `kmeans` repeats: each row to its nearest centroid, each centroid to the middle of its rows (the mean for the squared Euclidean distance, the median for city block), from k-means++ starts (`'Replicates'` runs it several times and keeps the best). It gives each row's cluster, the centroids, each cluster's total distance and each row's distances. `kmedoids` keeps the centres among the rows themselves (the medoids), which suits any distance and resists outliers.
syntax: [idx, C, sumd, D] = kmeans(X, k, 'Distance', d, 'Replicates', r)
[idx, C, sumd, D, midx] = kmedoids(X, k, 'Distance', d)

examples.title: Three groups found

pages.summary: Hierarchical clustering: a tree of merges, cut into clusters, and drawn.
body: `linkage` joins the two nearest clusters again and again: each row of Z joins two (the points numbered 1 to m, the merged clusters m+1, m+2, ...) at a height. How near is measured by the method: `'single'` (the closest pair, unless given), `'complete'`, `'average'`, `'weighted'`, `'centroid'`, `'median'` or `'ward'`. `cluster` cuts the tree into at most n clusters, or where links are inconsistent or high; `clusterdata` does both in one step. `dendrogram` draws the tree.
syntax: [H, T, outperm] = dendrogram(Z, P, 'ColorThreshold', t, 'Labels', names)

examples.title: Six cities by their coordinates

pages.summary: How well a tree keeps the distances, how inconsistent its links are, and the best order of its leaves.
body: `cophenet` gives the correlation between the original distances and the heights at which the tree first joins each pair (near 1 when the tree keeps them well). `inconsistent` compares each link's height with the links within d levels below it: a large coefficient marks a natural cut. `optimalleaforder` finds, among the orders the tree allows, the one with the least sum of distances between neighbouring leaves, for a dendrogram that reads better.
syntax: The correlation, and the tree's distances.

examples.title: Two methods compared

pages.summary: Clusters by density, and by the eigenvectors of a similarity graph.
body: `dbscan` grows clusters from core points, those with at least minpts points within epsilon, through their neighbours; points near no core point are noise (-1). It finds clusters of any shape and needs no number of them. `spectralcluster` joins each point to its nearest neighbours, weights the links by distance, and clusters the graph Laplacian's k eigenvectors of the smallest eigenvalues with k-means: it separates groups that are connected rather than round.

examples.title: Two rings that k-means cannot part

pages.summary: Gaussian mixtures: made, fitted to data, and the probability of each component for each point.
body: A Gaussian mixture is a weighted sum of normal distributions: means (a row each), covariances and proportions. `fitgmdist` fits one by expectation-maximization from k-means++ starts, with full or diagonal, shared or separate covariances and a regularization; it keeps the log-likelihood, AIC and BIC. `pdf`, `random`, `cluster`, `posterior` and `mahal` work on a mixture; `posterior` gives each component's probability given each point.
syntax: gm = fitgmdist(X, k, 'CovarianceType', t, 'SharedCovariance', tf, 'RegularizationValue', r, 'Replicates', n)

examples.title: Two components found again

pages.summary: Clusters cut from a hierarchical tree, or the clusters of a Gaussian mixture.
body: From a linkage tree: at most n clusters (`'MaxClust'`), or a cut where the inconsistency coefficient (or the height, with `'Criterion', 'distance'`) exceeds a cutoff; clusters are numbered in the order of their first observation. From a Gaussian mixture: each row goes with the component most probable for it, with the posterior probabilities and the negative log-likelihood.

examples.title: A tree cut two ways

pages.summary: How well points sit in their clusters, and the number of clusters a criterion prefers.
body: A point's silhouette is (b - a)/max(a, b), a its mean distance to the rest of its cluster and b to the nearest other cluster: near 1 for a point well inside its cluster, near 0 on a border, negative when it sits better in another; without outputs they are drawn as bars, cluster by cluster. `evalclusters` clusters for each k (by k-means, Ward linkage or a Gaussian mixture) and picks the k a criterion prefers: `'CalinskiHarabasz'`, `'DaviesBouldin'`, `'silhouette'` or `'gap'`.

examples.title: How many groups?

pages.summary: Principal components: the directions in which data vary most.
body: `pca` centres the data and takes its singular value decomposition: the components (coeff's columns, orthonormal), the data in their terms (score), their variances (latent), the percentage each explains, Hotelling's T² of each row and the means. Rows with NaN are left out; `'VariableWeights', 'variance'` works on standardized variables. `pcacov` gives the components of a covariance matrix; `barttest` tests how many components differ (whether the smallest eigenvalues may be equal).
syntax: [coeff, score, latent, tsquared, explained, mu] = pca(X, 'NumComponents', k)

pages.summary: Probabilistic principal components, missing values allowed.
body: The model Y = mu + X W' + noise of one variance, fitted by expectation-maximization, each row using the values it has (NaN is missing): the components, scores, their variances, the means and the noise variance, with the data reconstructed where values were missing.
syntax: [coeff, score, pcvar, mu, v, S] = ppca(Y, k)
With scores, variances, means, noise and more.

examples.title: A tenth of the values missing

pages.summary: Factor analysis, and loadings rotated to be simpler.
body: `factoran` models the variables' correlations as a few common factors plus each variable's own variance (lambda lambda' + diag(psi)), by maximum likelihood; the loadings are rotated (varimax unless named) so that each variable loads mostly on one factor. With the number of observations it tests whether m factors suffice. `rotatefactors` rotates loadings: orthogonally (varimax, quartimax, equamax, parsimax, orthomax), or obliquely (promax).
syntax: [lambda, psi, T, stats, F] = factoran(X, m, 'Rotate', method)
The loadings, specific variances, rotation, statistics and scores.

examples.title: Six tests, two abilities

pages.summary: Points placed so that their distances match given ones.
body: `cmdscale` (classical scaling) finds points whose Euclidean distances are D's exactly when D is Euclidean, and near them otherwise, with the eigenvalues that say how many dimensions are needed. `mdscale` fits points in p dimensions to dissimilarities: metric (the distances themselves) or nonmetric (only their order, `'stress'`, the default), measuring the misfit by Kruskal's stress.

examples.title: A map from road distances

pages.summary: Points in two (or three) dimensions whose neighbourhoods are those of high-dimensional data.
body: t-SNE matches each point's neighbourhood: Gaussian affinities in the data (their width set by the perplexity, 30) against Student t affinities among the points placed, by gradient descent. Groups that are apart in the data stay apart; distances between groups mean little.

examples.title: Three groups in ten dimensions

pages.summary: The rotation, scale and shift that fit one set of points onto another.
body: Z = b Y T + c fits X best by least squares; d is the residual sum of squares over X's (centred), 0 for a perfect fit. The transform holds T, b and c; `'Scaling'` false fixes b at 1, and `'Reflection'` allows (or forbids) a mirror image.
syntax: [d, Z, transform] = procrustes(X, Y, 'Scaling', tf, 'Reflection', tf)
With the fitted points and the transform.

examples.title: A shape found turned and shrunk

pages.summary: Canonical correlation: the combinations of two sets of variables most correlated with each other.
body: U = (X - mean) A and V = (Y - mean) B, each pair as correlated as it can be (r), each uncorrelated with the others, with unit variance. The statistics test, by Wilks' lambda and Bartlett's chi-square, whether the correlations from the k-th on are all zero.
syntax: [A, B, r, U, V, stats] = canoncorr(X, Y)

examples.title: Two sets sharing one signal

pages.summary: Nonnegative matrix factorization: A ≈ W H, nothing negative.
body: By alternating least squares (each solution's negatives set to zero) or multiplicative updates, from random starts (or W0 and H0), the best of several replicates; H's rows have unit length, and D is the root mean square residual. Parts that only add up (spectra of mixtures, counts) come out as parts.
syntax: [W, H, D] = nnmf(A, k, 'Algorithm', a, 'Replicates', r)

examples.title: Two spectra in mixtures

pages.summary: The correlation matrix of a covariance matrix.
body: R = C ./ (sigma sigma') with sigma the standard deviations, sqrt(diag(C)); a variable with zero variance gives NaN.
